# Continuous Recording

JFR has very low overhead, less than 1% impact on the application performance,
and can be kept running in the background. In this example we can see how JFR
can be kept running alongside the application, and how to collect the
information when required.

There are several ways to start the JFR and collect insights about a given Java
application, such as:

- [Using JDK Mission Control (JMC)](#continuous-recording-using-jdk-mission-control-jmc)
- [Using `jcmd`](#continuous-recording-using-jcmd)
- [During application start time](#continuous-recording-when-starting-the-application)
- [Programmatically](#continuous-recording-programmatically)

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [JDK Mission Control (JMC)](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

## JDK Mission Control (JMC)

1. Download the latest version of JMC from
   [here](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/products-jmc9-downloads.html)

2. Specify the version of Java

   When having multiple versions of Java installed, you may need to specify
   which one to be used by JMC. This can be done through the `jmc.ini` file,
   found under the `Eclipse` directory of where JMC is installed.

   Add the `-vm` option followed by the path to the `bin` directory, as shown
   next.

   ```
   ...
   -vm
   /Users/aattard/.sdkman/candidates/java/current/bin
   ...
   ```

   Please note that this file will contain other information, which is excluded
   for brevity.

## Build the application

The following examples require the application to be built.

```shell
./mvnw clean package
```

(*Optional*) Verify that the JAR file was created

```shell
tree --sort=name './target/libs'
```

There should be one JAR file

```
./target/libs
└── continuous-recording-1.0.0.jar

1 directory, 1 file
```

Some of the following commands dump JFR files into a `jfr` directory. Make sure
that the `jfr` directory exists.

```shell
rm -rf './jfr'
mkdir -p './jfr'
```

## Continuous Recording using JDK Mission Control (JMC)

1. Start the application

   While it is not important to run the application in the background, it’s
   convenient as you don’t have to switch to another terminal window.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/libs/continuous-recording-1.0.0.jar' > './target/continuous-recording-jmc.log' 2>&1 &

   # Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
   echo "$!" > './target/continuous-recording-jmc.pid'
   ```

   The application will run until interrupted (killed).

2. Start the flight recording

   ![Start recording](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Start%20recording.png)

   Select the *Continuous recording* option, and click *Finish*.

3. Allow recording data to be collected

   ![Allow recording data to be collected](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Allow%20recording%20data%20to%20be%20collected.png)

4. Dump JFR recording

   ![Dump JFR recording](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Dump%20JFR%20recording%201.png)

   Provide the *Time span* and click *Finish*

   ![Dump JFR recording](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20Dump%20JFR%20recording%202.png)

5. View the recording

   ![View recording](./assets/images/JMC%20-%20View%20recording.png)

6. Close the application when ready

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/continuous-recording-jmc.pid')"
   ```

## Continuous Recording using `jcmd`

1. Start the application

   While it is not important to run the application in the background, it’s
   convenient as you don’t have to switch to another terminal window.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/libs/continuous-recording-1.0.0.jar' > './target/continuous-recording-jcmd.log' 2>&1 &

   # Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
   echo "$!" > './target/continuous-recording-jcmd.pid'
   ```

   The application will run until interrupted (killed).

2. (*Optional*) Identify the Java application PID

   ```shell
   jcmd
   ```

   This lists all Java applications running on this machine, including the
   `jcmd` command.

   ```
   123457 jdk.jcmd/sun.tools.jcmd.JCmd
   123456 ./target/libs/continuous-recording-1.0.0.jar
   ```

   The PID for this application was saved when the process was started and can
   be displayed using the following command.

   ```shell
   cat './target/continuous-recording-jcmd.pid'
   ```

   This will print just the PID

   ```
   123456
   ```

3. Start JFR using `jcmd`

   Note how the saved PID is reused and then passed to the `jcmd` command to
   start JFR.

   ```shell
   PID="$(cat './target/continuous-recording-jcmd.pid')"
   jcmd "${PID}" \
     JFR.start \
     name='Continuous-Recording' \
     filename='./jfr/demo-jcmd.jfr'
   ```

   This will print just the PID and a message saying that the recording has
   started.

   ```
   123456:
   Started recording 1. No limit specified, using maxsize=250MB as default.

   Use jcmd 123456 JFR.dump name=Continuous-Recording to copy recording data to file.
   ```

   Instead of `$(cat './target/continuous-recording-jcmd.pid')`, you can use
   the PID directly (`123456` in this example), as shown next

   ```
   $ jcmd 123456 \
     JFR.start \
     name='Continuous-Recording' \
     filename='./jfr/demo-jcmd.jfr'
   ```

   Make sure that the directories (`./jfr` in this example) where the JFR file
   (`demo-jcmd.jfr` in this example) is saved exists, as otherwise the
   application will fail to start.

4. Dump JFR recording

   Wait a few seconds before dumping the recording as otherwise it may be empty.

   ```shell
   sleep 30
   ```

   Dump the recording for our application.

   ```shell
   PID="$(cat './target/continuous-recording-jcmd.pid')"
   jcmd "${PID}" \
     JFR.dump \
     filename='./jfr/demo-jcmd-dump.jfr'
   ```

   Dump the recording in a different file so that this is not updated when the
   application is closed.

5. (*Optional*) Verify that the file was created as expected.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The recordings

   ```
   ./jfr
   ├── demo-jcmd-dump.jfr
   └── demo-jcmd.jfr

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

6. Close the application when ready.

   No need to keep the application running once the dump has been generated.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/continuous-recording-jcmd.pid')"
   ```

7. Open the recording file (`./jfr/demo-jcmd-dump.jfr`), in JDK Mission Control.

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-jcmd-dump.jfr"
   ```

## Continuous Recording when starting the application

1. Start the application using the `-XX:StartFlightRecording` option, without
   providing the `duration` option.

   While it is not important to run the application in the background, it’s
   convenient as you don’t have to switch to another terminal window.

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:StartFlightRecording=name='Continuous-Recording',filename='./jfr/demo-cla.jfr' \
     -jar './target/libs/continuous-recording-1.0.0.jar' > './target/continuous-recording-cla.log' 2>&1 &

   # Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
   echo "$!" > './target/continuous-recording-cla.pid'
   ```

   The application will simply until interrupted (killed).

2. Dump the JFR recording using [JMC](#continuous-recording-using-jdk-mission-control-jmc)
   or [`jcmd`](#continuous-recording-using-jcmd).

   Wait a few seconds before dumping the recording as otherwise it may be empty.

   ```shell
   sleep 30
   ```

   Dump the recording for our application.

   ```shell
   PID="$(cat './target/continuous-recording-cla.pid')"
   jcmd "${PID}" \
     JFR.dump \
     filename='./jfr/demo-cla-dump.jfr'
   ```

   Dump the recording in a different file so that this is not updated when the
   application is closed.

3. (*Optional*) Verify that the file was created as expected.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The recordings.

   ```
   ./jfr
   ├── demo-cla-dump.jfr
   ├── demo-cla.jfr
   ├── demo-jcmd-dump.jfr
   └── demo-jcmd.jfr

   1 directory, 4 files
   ```

4. Close the application when ready.

   No need to keep the application running once the dump has been generated.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/continuous-recording-cla.pid')"
   ```

5. Open the recording file (`./jfr/demo-cla-dump.jfr`), in JDK Mission Control.

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-cla-dump.jfr"
   ```

## Continuous Recording Programmatically

The flight recording can be started programmatically, as shown in the following
code fragment. Note that the `Recording` takes a `Configuration`, and we are
using the default configuration. We will come back to this at a later stage. For
the time being just note that JFR is very customizable, and we can collect the
data we need at the level we need it. The default configuration provides the
right balance between amount of information and performance overhead (under 1%),
which makes it ideal for production use.

```java
try (Recording recording = new Recording(Configuration.getConfiguration("default"))) {
    recording.setDestination(Path.of("./jfr/demo-programmatically.jfr"));
    recording.setName("Start-JFR");
    recording.start();

    /* Wait while capturing the events and saved the to the recording. */
    System.out.println("The application will terminate automatically in about 40 seconds");
    TimeUnit.SECONDS.sleep(40);
}
/* The recording is completed and written to file. */
/* No more events are captured by this recording. */
```

1. Update the code

   Copy the updated version of the code from the `fixtures/01-programmatically/`
   directory.

   ```shell
   rsync --archive 'fixtures/01-programmatically/' .
   ```

   The [`Main` class](./src/main/java/demo/Main.java) should look like the
   following example.

   ```java
   package demo;

   import module java.base;
   import module jdk.jfr;

   import jdk.jfr.Configuration;

   public final class Main {

       static void main() throws Exception {
           try (Recording recording = new Recording(Configuration.getConfiguration("default"))) {
               recording.setDestination(Path.of("./jfr/demo-programmatically.jfr"));
               recording.setName("Start-JFR");
               recording.start();

               /* Wait while capturing the events and saved the to the recording. */
               System.out.println("The application will terminate automatically in about 40 seconds");
               TimeUnit.SECONDS.sleep(40);
           }
           /* The recording is completed and written to file. */
           /* No more events are captured by this recording. */
       }
   }
   ```

2. Rebuild the application.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

3. Run the application without providing any JFR related options.

   While it is not important to run the application in the background, it’s
   convenient as you don’t have to switch to another terminal window.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/libs/continuous-recording-1.0.0.jar'
   ```

   The application will simply wait 40 seconds, and it will then exist.

4. (*Optional*) Verify that the file was created as expected.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './jfr'
   ```

   The recordings.

   ```
   ./jfr
   ├── demo-cla-dump.jfr
   ├── demo-cla.jfr
   ├── demo-jcmd-dump.jfr
   ├── demo-jcmd.jfr
   └── demo-programmatically.jfr

   1 directory, 5 files
   ```

5. Open the recording file (`./jfr/demo-programmatically-dump.jfr`), in JDK Mission
   Control.

   ```shell
   jmc -open "$(pwd)/jfr/demo-programmatically-dump.jfr"
   ```
